name: Hooray SourceSignal for Google Preferred Sources
author: hoorayplugins

sections.description:
Google Preferred Sources for WordPress — without the code

Google Preferred Sources can help readers see more of your content in Google Search.

SourceSignal makes it easy to add Preferred Sources buttons and prompts to your WordPress site — without editing code or hiring a developer.

Install the plugin, choose what you want the button to look like and where you want it to appear, and turn it on.

That’s it.

Built by a publisher, for publishers

I run a small independent publishing company. We don’t have an in-house development team.

When Google launched Preferred Sources, I wanted it on our sites. The basic Google code looked simple enough. Making it work the way I wanted across WordPress, different placements, mobile devices, caching and our existing site setup was another story.

So we built SourceSignal.

The goal was simple: make Google Preferred Sources something a publisher can set up in a few minutes instead of another project to send to a developer.

We use it on our own publishing sites, and we’ve tested it on real WordPress sites and browsers.

What you can do with SourceSignal

  • Add Google Preferred Sources without touching code. No snippets, no theme files, no CSS.
  • Choose how it looks. Google’s official button, a card, an inline button, a text link, your own design, or a button you already have.
  • Choose where it appears. Automatically before or after articles, or place a block or the [preferred_source] shortcode yourself.
  • Control where it shows. Limit automatic placement to the post types and categories you choose.
  • Preview everything before turning it on. The wizard and settings screen show the real button, not a mock-up. Nothing changes for readers until you press Turn it on.
  • Avoid annoying repeat visitors. Hide it for a while after someone uses it or closes it.
  • Works with page caching and CDNs. Every visitor gets the same HTML; the reader’s browser decides whether to show it.
  • Falls back gracefully if Google’s script isn’t available. Readers still get a link to Google’s Source Preferences page.

A note about Google

SourceSignal helps you promote Google’s Preferred Sources feature. Google controls the feature and the final selection happens on Google’s side.

Google does not provide publishers with confirmation that an individual reader completed the selection, so SourceSignal does not report clicks as confirmed Preferred Source adds.

SourceSignal is an independent publisher tool and is not affiliated with or endorsed by Google.

Want to promote Preferred Sources beyond your website?

We’re also building SourceSignal Pro for publishers who want to promote Preferred Sources through newsletters, social media and print.

Pro adds publisher-controlled campaign links, printable QR codes, campaign management and reporting for the parts of the funnel we can actually measure — including views, clicks and Google-flow launches.

Pro is coming soon.

External services

To open Google’s Preferred Sources screen, this plugin loads Google’s publisher library from https://news.google.com/swg/js/v1/publisher.js.

When it loads: on pages that carry a Preferred Sources button or prompt — or, if you switch on “Let buttons added outside the block editor open the card too”, on every page of your site. That setting is off unless you turn it on, and the settings screen tells you which state your site is in.

What Google receives: loading that file is a request to Google, so Google receives what any web request carries — the reader’s IP address, their browser, and the address of the page they are on. If you use Google’s own rendered button, Google also draws it inside a frame served from Google, and that frame receives the address of the article the reader is on.

The fallback: when Google’s library cannot load, or JavaScript is switched off, the prompt becomes a plain link to Google’s Source Preferences page, https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=yourdomain.com. It is written into the page but only requested if a reader follows it.

Google’s handling of any of this is governed by Google’s own terms and privacy policy, not by this plugin:

  • Terms: https://policies.google.com/terms
  • Privacy: https://policies.google.com/privacy

Privacy

Nothing about readers is stored on your server. There is no reader table, no event log, no identifier, no analytics, and nothing is sent to the plugin’s author.

In the reader’s own browser, when they press or close a Preferred Sources button or prompt, the plugin saves a date stamp — in local storage and in a first-party cookie of the same name:

  • psfp_used_at — the reader pressed it.
  • psfp_closed_at — the reader closed it.

Each holds a date and nothing else: no name, no account, no identifier. The cookie is set with path=/ and SameSite=Lax, and expires by itself after the window you chose. Nothing is written merely because a reader was shown the prompt, and nothing at all is written if both windows are set to “Keep showing it”. Your server never reads either copy, which is what keeps page caching working — though the cookies travel with ordinary page requests the way every cookie does.

It is per browser, not per person: the same reader on a phone and a laptop counts twice, and clearing site data resets it.

WordPress’s Settings → Privacy screen carries a suggested paragraph for your own privacy policy, generated from your site’s own settings. It is a starting point, not legal advice.

The plugin’s settings live in two options, psfp_settings and psfp_setup, plus a 60-second marker after activation. Uninstalling removes all three, from every site on a network, and leaves your posts alone.
sections.installation:
1. Install and activate the plugin. Nothing changes for readers yet.
  2. WordPress opens Set up Preferred Sources. (If it does not, open Preferred Sources → Setup from the admin menu.)
  3. Answer the questions — where it should appear, on what content, how it should look, what it should say — watching the preview beside them.
  4. Press Turn it on on the last step.
  5. If your site uses a caching plugin or a CDN, clear its cache.

To place it by hand instead, add the Preferred Sources block to any post or page. In the editor, search for “preferred source”.
sections.faq:
How do I add Google Preferred Sources to WordPress?

Install this plugin, answer the setup questions, look at the preview, and press Turn it on. You can also drop the Preferred Sources block into a post (search “preferred source” in the editor), or use the [preferred_source] shortcode. You do not edit a theme or paste Google’s script yourself.

Do I need to add Google’s JavaScript manually?

No. The plugin loads Google’s publisher library on pages that need it, and leaves it off pages that do not.

Can I add a Preferred Sources button without a developer?

Yes. That is the point. Install it, choose where it appears and how it looks, preview it, turn it on. No PHP, no JavaScript, no templates.

Does it work with caching plugins and CDNs?

It is built so full-page caches stay safe: every visitor gets the same HTML, and whether a particular reader sees the prompt is decided in their browser. We used it on real publisher sites that run caches and advertising technology. Clear your cache after you change a setting. We do not claim it never glitches on every stack.

Can I control which articles or categories show it?

Yes. Automatic placement can run before or after articles, on the post types you choose, and — for posts — only in, or except in, the categories you choose. Choosing a category includes its subcategories. You can also place a block or shortcode by hand and leave automatic placement off.

Can I use Preferred Sources links in email or social media?

Not in this Free 1.0.0 release. Free puts Preferred Sources buttons and prompts on your WordPress site. Campaign links, QR codes for print and reporting on those promotions are part of SourceSignal Pro, which is coming soon.

Does SourceSignal know whether someone actually added my publication?

No. Google does not give the plugin a reliable confirmation that a reader finished the final Preferred Sources selection. Free can remember that a browser pressed the button or closed it. That is not a confirmed add, a conversion or a follower count.

Will this improve my rankings or bring me traffic?

Nobody can promise that, and this plugin does not. Google controls Preferred Sources and decides what it does with a reader’s choices.

Which publication will Google ask readers to prefer?

Whichever site the page is served from. Google’s script works the publication out from the page’s own address; there is no setting in Google’s library — or here — that can point it at a different one. The plugin’s domain box only changes the fallback link a reader gets when JavaScript is unavailable.

What does “hide it for 90 days” actually remember?

That this browser pressed the button, or closed it. It is kept in the reader’s own browser — in local storage and in a cookie of the same name, psfp_used_at and psfp_closed_at — and is never read by your server, which is what keeps page caching working. It is per browser rather than per person, so the same reader on a phone and a laptop counts twice, and clearing site data resets it. Nothing is stored at all if you set both windows to “Keep showing it”.

Nothing appears on my articles.

Check, in order: the status line at the top of the settings screen (“Automatic placement is off…” or “…is on: at the end of Posts, in every category.”); that the content type you are looking at is ticked; that a category rule is not excluding it (“Only posts in the categories I choose” with nothing ticked means no post gets one); your cache; and finally your own browser — if you have already pressed or closed a prompt here, you are being left alone on purpose. A private window shows it again.

Google’s own button is empty.

Google draws that button itself, and it will not draw one for an address that is not a public publication — a local or staging site, for instance. The settings screen warns you when your address looks like one. The plugin deliberately does not put its own link beside an empty Google slot, because on a live site that guess sat next to a working Google button. Use one of the plugin’s own presentations if you would rather not depend on Google’s drawing.

What happens if Google’s script is blocked?

The prompt falls back to a link to Google’s own preferences page, opened in a new tab so the reader keeps their place. With JavaScript switched off entirely, that link is what the reader gets in the first place.

Can I use my own button design?

Yes, three ways. Choose “Your own design” in the block for colors and spacing without CSS. Build the button with the core Button block and tick “Open the preferred sources card” in its sidebar — it keeps every styling control your theme gives you. Or, for a button that is not a core Button block (Kadence Blocks, Elementor, Divi, a theme element), put the class psfp-trigger in that block’s own “additional CSS class” field.

Does it work with my theme?

It inherits your theme’s fonts and colors and sets nothing globally. Tested at desktop and phone widths with Twenty Twenty-Five, Twenty Twenty-Four and Twenty Twenty-One, and against a stylesheet written to fight back. Kadence and Kadence Blocks were exercised in an earlier test environment. That is not the same as “works everywhere”.

What if my theme already loads Google’s publisher library?

A copy loaded through WordPress’s own script system is detected, and the plugin does not add a second one. A copy printed straight into the theme’s header cannot be seen from PHP, so both tags end up on the page — Google’s library ignores the second load, and everything still works.

Does it work on multisite?

Each site on a network keeps its own settings, and uninstalling removes them from every site. Beyond that the plugin gives multisite no special handling, and it has not been exercised on a production network.

Has this been tested on phones and in-app browsers?

Google’s own button and the plugin’s own prompts have both been used on a real iPhone — in Safari and in the Gmail, Yahoo Mail and Facebook in-app browsers — and on desktop Chrome, on one live publication. Both opened Google’s Preferred Sources flow, and an add was completed. Android phones, the Instagram and Outlook in-app browsers, and any second publication have not been tested. The rest of the matrix is desktop and phone-sized automated browsers.

What happens when I delete the plugin?

Its own settings are removed, from every site on a network. Your posts are left alone: a block or a shortcode you wrote into an article is your writing, and the plugin will not edit it out.
sections.changelog:
1.0.0

  • A setup wizard: eight plain questions, a live preview, and a last step that turns it on. Nothing changes on your site until that step, and an existing install is never redirected into it.
  • The preview on the settings screen and in the wizard now follows every change instantly, including the presentation, rendered by the same code as the front end.
  • Automatic placement can be limited to, or kept out of, particular categories.
  • A suggested privacy-policy paragraph under Settings → Privacy, written for the site’s own settings.
  • Alignment now moves Google’s own button as well as the plugin’s presentations.
  • Nothing is written to a reader’s browser when both “asking again” windows are set to “Keep showing it”.
  • The settings screen says what was corrected when a colour, domain or language tag could not be used, reminds you about page caches after a save, and states plainly when Google’s library is being loaded on every page.
  • Uninstalling now also removes the record of whether setup was run.
  • A backslash typed into the heading, text or button label now survives saving; a suppression window set outside the dropdown’s choices (for example from WP-CLI) is no longer reset to “Keep showing it” on the next save.

0.2.0

  • Google’s own button is left alone. The plugin no longer waits six seconds, guesses whether Google’s control rendered, and adds its own link beside it — a live beta showed that guess was wrong on a working button in every browser it was tried in, including one already reading “Added to Preferred Sources”.
  • The link beside Google’s button is now shown only when Google’s library never loads at all, which is the one case where there is definitely no button to press.
  • Asset version bumped so browsers and CDNs pick up the new script and stylesheet rather than a cached 0.1.0 copy.

0.1.0

  • First release.
  • Close button on the card and “your own design” presentations, so the “hide it after a reader closes it” setting has something to act on.
  • Google’s own button falls back to a link if the library never fills its slot.
  • Automatic placement stays out of excerpts and out of query loops inside an article.
  • Automatic placement stands down on an article that already contains a block or shortcode — the one the publisher placed wins.
